payload.title: Block released from a height that stops on a rough section

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=0.5\text{ kg}$ is released from rest at a height $h=0.8\text{ m}$ above a horizontal floor on a smooth, frictionless curved track. At the bottom of the track the block slides onto a rough horizontal section whose coefficient of kinetic friction is $\mu=0.2$. The rough section is long enough that the block comes to rest on it. Blank energy bar chart templates (one per state, with a common scale) are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: In the energy bar charts below, for each of three states (the block at the release point, the block at the bottom of the track just before the rough section, and the block at rest on the rough section), draw bars for the kinetic energy $K$, the gravitational potential energy $U_g$ (zero at the floor), and the energy dissipated by friction as thermal energy $E_{th}$. Use the same scale in each chart.
parts.model_answer: At the release point: $U_g=mgh=3.92\text{ J}$, $K=0$, $E_{th}=0$. At the bottom: $K=3.92\text{ J}$, $U_g=0$. At rest on the rough section: $K=0$, $U_g=0$, and $E_{th}=3.92\text{ J}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Shows only $U_g$ (no $K$ and no $E_{th}$) at the release point
common_errors: shows kinetic energy at the release point

rubric_rows.criterion: Shows $K$ equal in height to the initial $U_g$ with $U_g=0$ and $E_{th}=0$ at the bottom of the track
common_errors: shows thermal energy on the frictionless track

rubric_rows.criterion: Shows $K=0$, $U_g=0$, and $E_{th}$ equal in height to the initial $U_g$ when the block is at rest
common_errors: shows the thermal energy smaller than the initial potential energy

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the distance $d$ the block slides on the rough section before it stops in terms of $h$, $\mu$, and fundamental constants.
parts.model_answer: Energy conservation on the track gives $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$; the work of friction on the rough section removes it all, $\mu mgd=\tfrac12mv^2$. Together $\mu mgd=mgh$ so $d=h/\mu$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses conservation of energy on the track: $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$ (or $v=\sqrt{2gh}$) at the bottom
common_errors: uses mgh = mv

rubric_rows.criterion: Equates the work done by friction to the kinetic energy lost on the rough section: $\mu mgd=\tfrac12mv^2$
required_elements: mu m g d = 1/2 m v^2
common_errors: omits the normal force in the friction work

rubric_rows.criterion: Combines the equations to the correct expression $d=h/\mu$

payload.title: Claim about the friction force needed on a flat curve

stimulus.description: A car of mass $m=1000\text{ kg}$ drives at a constant speed around a flat, unbanked circular curve of radius $r=40\text{ m}$. parts.prompt: Do you agree or disagree with the student's claim? Justify your answer qualitatively without calculating numbers.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. The friction force from the road is the net force toward the center of the circle and must equal $mv^2/r$, which depends on the square of the speed, so doubling the speed requires more than double the friction force.

accepted_answers: The submerged fraction increases. The total weight of the block and coin is larger, so a larger buoyant force is needed for the block to stay at rest, which requires a larger submerged volume.

difficulty.rationale: Standard floating-equilibrium FRQ: apply F_B = mg to evaluate a flawed claim (qualitative), derive V_sub/V = rho_b/rho and compute one simple ratio (about 0.69), then predict the effect of added load on the submerged fraction.
